quiz: A raw counter only ever goes up. Ask which query turns it into a speed per second, and in which order the functions should be applied.
An average mixes fast and slow requests into one number. Ask which measurement would reveal a small group of very slow requests.
A safe label has a small, fixed set of values that you control and that does not grow with traffic.
The number of series is the product of the number of values of each label.
Ask which numbers can be added together across pods without losing the full distribution of requests.
Think of the for: clause as a timer started by the first true evaluation. Ask what happens to that timer when the condition breaks once.
Picture one big outage that fires many related alerts. Ask what Alertmanager can do so people get only the most important one.
Ask how long a silence should last and who should be able to see it. What happens to a problem that stays hidden forever?
Recall the W3C Trace Context standard header that holds version, trace id, parent span id and flags.
The root span covers the whole request, so it is always long. Ask which number tells you where time is actually spent.
Think about when each sampler decides: at the very start of a trace, or after seeing the whole trace and its errors.
Burn rate equals the observed error ratio divided by the error budget, which is 1 minus the SLO.
The long window shows the loss is big. Think about what the short window proves about the problem right now.
Ask how long a value stays in git history once it is committed, and who gets a copy of it. Then pick the option that avoids that.
Ask what kind of data must never reach a shared log store, and where the earliest point is that you can strip it out.

Show summing bucket rates by le before histogram_quantile, explain linear interpolation inside a bucket, and how bucket width limits accuracy.

Compare who operates it, cost shape, speed to value, lock-in and data rules, and say when each option fits a team.
